title: "Getting started"
---

This page goes through one decision from start to finish: install the client, save your token, see what you may trade, download prices, build a portfolio, check it and submit it. The client packages are the same in R and Python: same functions, same column names. Pick your language in any tab; every tab on the page follows.

## 1. Install

In a terminal, in your project folder:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

With [uvr](https://github.com/nbafrank/uvr), version 0.4.8 or later (`uvr --version` shows yours, `uvr upgrade` updates it). The folder has to be a uvr project: if it has no `uvr.toml` yet, run `uvr init` first.

```sh
uvr add advanced-empirical-finance/aefsim/r tidyfinance dplyr tidyr
```

Then restart R, so it picks up the new packages.

## Python

With [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). The folder has to be a uv project: if it has no `pyproject.toml` yet, run `uv init` first.

```sh
uv add "git+https://github.com/advanced-empirical-finance/aefsim#subdirectory=python" tidyfinance
```

:::

## 2. Save your token

Your team receives one token, starting with `aef_`: the key with which the client authenticates your team to the trading game. Treat it like a password: it lets anyone trade for your team. Run `set_token()` once and paste the token when asked:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```r
library(aefsim)
library(tidyfinance)
library(dplyr)

set_token()   # once per project
```

## Python

```python
import datetime as dt

import aefsim
import polars as pl
import tidyfinance as tf

aefsim.set_token()  # once per project
```

:::

It asks where to save the token: `project` for your project's folder or `home` for your home folder. For a project folder, it offers to add the file to `.gitignore`, so the token never ends up in Git. From then on the client finds the token by itself, in every new session too. Don't put the token in your code.

## 3. What can you trade, and under which rules?

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```r
universe <- get_universe()
close_date <- max(universe$close_date)   # the latest close
count(universe, sp500)

get_parameters()                    # costs, shorting, leverage; applies_next marks the current rules
get_calendar() |> filter(is_next)   # the next trading day and its deadline
```

## Python

```python
universe = aefsim.get_universe()
close_date = universe["close_date"].max()  # the latest close
universe.group_by("sp500").len()

aefsim.get_parameters()                            # costs, shorting, leverage; applies_next marks the current rules
aefsim.get_calendar().filter(pl.col("is_next"))  # the next trading day and its deadline
```

:::

`get_universe()` lists the asset universe, the stocks you can buy after the latest close: common stocks on NYSE, NYSE American and Nasdaq that closed at $5 or more. Each comes with its CRSP `permno`, so a portfolio you build from CRSP data, such as tidyfinance's `crsp_monthly`, maps to tickers with a join on `permno`. A stock you hold that drops below $5 stays in your portfolio; you may keep or reduce it, but not buy more.

## 4. Download prices

For the example, tidyfinance downloads a year of prices from Yahoo Finance, the source the trading game trades at.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```r
candidates <- universe |> filter(sp500) |> pull(ticker)
prices <- download_data("stock_prices", symbols = candidates,
                        start_date = close_date - 365, end_date = close_date)
```

## Python

```python
candidates = universe.filter(pl.col("sp500"))["ticker"].to_list()
prices = tf.download_data(
    domain="stock_prices",
    symbols=candidates,
    start_date=str(close_date - dt.timedelta(days=365)),
    end_date=str(close_date),
)
```

:::

## 5. Build a portfolio

As an example, not a recommendation: the 20 S&P 500 stocks with the lowest volatility over the past year, equal weight.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```r
weights <- prices |>
  arrange(symbol, date) |>
  group_by(symbol) |>
  mutate(ret = adjusted_close / lag(adjusted_close) - 1) |>
  summarise(vol = sd(ret, na.rm = TRUE) * sqrt(252), days = n()) |>
  filter(days >= 200) |>
  slice_min(vol, n = 20) |>
  transmute(ticker = symbol, weight = 1 / n())
weights
```

## Python

```python
volatility = (
    prices.sort("symbol", "date")
    .with_columns(ret=pl.col("adjusted_close").pct_change().over("symbol"))
    .group_by("symbol")
    .agg(vol=pl.col("ret").std() * 252 ** 0.5, days=pl.len())
    .filter(pl.col("days") >= 200)
    .sort("vol")
    .head(20)
)
weights = volatility.select(ticker="symbol", weight=pl.lit(1 / volatility.height))
weights
```

:::

Your weight vector is a data frame with the columns `ticker` and `weight`: each weight is the fraction of your portfolio's value in that stock, negative for a short position. Stocks you leave out get weight zero, so this replaces your whole portfolio; whatever does not add up to one stays in cash.

## 6. Check, then submit

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```r
validate(weights, close_date = close_date)   # every check, nothing stored

result <- submit(
  weights, close_date = close_date,
  rationale = "Low-volatility tilt: equal weight in the 20 least volatile S&P 500 stocks over the past year."
)
result
```

## Python

```python
aefsim.validate(weights, close_date=close_date)  # every check, nothing stored

result = aefsim.submit(
    weights,
    close_date=close_date,
    rationale="Low-volatility tilt: equal weight in the 20 least volatile S&P 500 stocks over the past year.",
)
result
```

:::

`validate()` runs every check the trading game runs and stores nothing. That's all you do: **the trade happens automatically** at the next market open whose deadline, 09:00 New York time (usually 15:00 in Copenhagen), has not passed; the check shows that date. The rationale is your decision log: write down what you expect and why.

Changed your mind? Submit again before the deadline: the new submission simply replaces the previous one. Or withdraw it with `cancel(result$submission_id)` in R, `aefsim.cancel(result.submission_id)` in Python.

## 7. The next morning

Trades happen at the US open; results appear after the nightly update.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```r
get_submissions()                             # status, trade date, rationale, weights
get_portfolio() |> tidyr::unnest(positions)   # one row per position, with portfolio value and cash
get_performance()                             # your daily portfolio value and statistics, next to the benchmarks
get_leaderboard()                             # every team under its pseudonym
```

## Python

```python
aefsim.get_submissions()                                          # status, trade date, rationale, weights
aefsim.get_portfolio().explode("positions").unnest("positions")   # one row per position
aefsim.get_performance()                                          # your daily portfolio value and statistics, next to the benchmarks
aefsim.get_leaderboard()                                          # every team under its pseudonym
```

:::

Your team's [dashboard](dashboard.qmd) shows the same in charts.

## When something goes wrong

Every message says what went wrong and what to do, and ends with a code in brackets. A check or a rejected submission lists every problem at once, for example:

```
Check: problems found
Trades at the open on 2027-02-10 (rules P1-baseline)
Positions 21, gross 1.050, net 1.050, cash -0.050
Errors:
  unknown_ticker BRKB: Not a stock in the trading game on 2027-02-09. Check the spelling: the trading game uses Yahoo tickers, and share classes take a hyphen, as in BRK-B. get_universe() lists the stocks you can buy.
  net_exposure_exceeded: The weights add up to 1.05 (net exposure); the limit is 1.00. They may add up to less: the rest of the book stays in cash.
```
